item.title: Language Entropy - v1.0.3 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Short Description:
Scores text fields against bigram language models to detect strings atypical for a language — random names, DGA domains, hashes, and other machine-generated sequences.


Description:
The Apius Language Entropy app measures how well any string matches the character patterns of a given language. Its custom search command computes bigram cross-entropy against trained language models: strings built from natural, language-typical character sequences receive low scores, while random-looking or machine-generated strings — hashes, tokens, encoded payloads, algorithmically generated names — stand out with high scores. Unlike plain Shannon entropy, which only measures character distribution within a string, cross-entropy scoring evaluates strings against real language statistics, reliably separating genuine words from random sequences built from the same characters. Scoring works with any language: the app ships with a Polish (default) and English bigram models and lets you build and upload models for other languages from simple frequency files through its web interface. Scoring the same field against multiple models also reveals which language a string most likely belongs to. Typical applications include security use cases such as detecting DGA domains, DNS tunneling, and C2 traffic hiding behind random-looking names, as well as broader data-quality and anomaly-detection scenarios: spotting machine-generated identifiers where human-given names are expected, flagging encoded or obfuscated content in logs, and filtering garbage values in text fields. The app includes the entropy streaming search command (usable in any SPL pipeline), a model-management page for converting bigram frequency files into ready-to-use probability models, and an interactive Entropy Lab for scoring individual strings or batch files, tuning thresholds with per-model summary statistics, and exporting results to CSV.

Edits are blocked when required keys are missing. \- Adds configurable source and output app/lookup settings, display-order ranges, and per-panel mode tokens for dashboards containing multiple forms. \- Loads legacy responses that do not contain batch IDs or saved field metadata and retains the established form\_viz/form\_responses defaults. \- Handles duplicate question labels and missing order values independently, refreshes dependent searches only after confirmed writes, and displays actionable configuration and load errors. \- Improves token handling, direct-load limits, stale-request protection, resize stability, upgrade rollback, automated compatibility testing, and release validation. \- Replaces the crowded app navigation with an explanatory home dashboard and two focused Create and Review/Edit examples. Compatibility: Splunk Enterprise Classic Dashboards. Dashboard Studio is not supported in this V2 release.


Short Description:
Form Viz adds an interactive form visualization for Splunk Classic Dashboards, turning SPL results into form inputs and saving structured responses to KV Store for reporting, review, and workflow use.


Description:
Form Viz is a custom Splunk visualization for building interactive forms directly from SPL results or lookup-driven configuration. It solves the problem of collecting structured analyst input inside Splunk dashboards without building custom web pages or external apps. Form Viz can render text fields, dropdowns, radio buttons, checkboxes, dates, numbers, markdown guidance, and SPL review fields from simple rows containing question, type, options, order, and description values. Submitted responses are written to a Splunk KV Store collection with user, form name, question order, question text, answer, timestamp, and submission ID fields. This makes it useful for review workflows, triage forms, detection validation, saved search reviews, analyst notes, and other dashboard-based data collection tasks. The app includes example dashboards showing how to configure forms, use SPL display/input fields, and run a multi-section Saved Search Review workflow.

item.description:

Release Notes:
**# Release Notes: TA-suhlabs-eMASS v1.0.6** **\*\*Release Date:\*\*** 2026-08-07 **\*\*UCC Framework Version:\*\*** 6.5.2 **## Overview** Version 1.0.6 is a maintenance and compatibility release that upgrades the UCC framework to version 6.5.2, officially declares compatibility with Splunk 10.x (dropping 9.x), adds standard Splunk app icons, and cleans up deprecated custom Mako templates to ensure complete AppInspect compliance. **## New Features** \- **\*\*Splunk 10.x Compatibility\*\***: Official compatibility declared for Splunk 10.x. Docker and demo configurations have been updated to use the latest Splunk versions. Compatibility with Splunk 9.x has been dropped. \- **\*\*Splunk App Icons\*\***: Integrated standard Splunk application icons (\`appIcon.png\` and \`appIcon\_2x.png\`) under both \`package/appserver/static/\` and \`package/static/\` to ensure visual presence in launcher and apps lists. \- **\*\*GitHub Dependabot\*\***: Enabled automated dependency tracking and security alerts via Dependabot. **## Bug Fixes & Hardening** \- **\*\*AppInspect Compliance (Mako Templates)\*\***: Deleted deprecated custom HTML template \`package/appserver/templates/base.html\` to guarantee clean AppInspect vetting with zero custom Mako templates. \- **\*\*Agent Rules Alignment\*\***: Standardized engineering constraints and project rules in \`.agents/rules/\` for developer tooling consistency. \- **\*\*zip\_ta.sh — Exclusion Hardening\*\***: Enhanced packaging exclusions to prevent packaging volume-mounted \`default.old.\*\` stanzas. **## Dependency Updates** \- Upgraded \`splunk-add-on-ucc-framework\` from \`6.1.0\` to \`6.5.2\`. **## Upgrade Notes** \- Rebuild and repackage required: \`make build && make zip\` \- No configuration schema changes or migration steps are needed. **## Verified On** \- Splunk Enterprise: 10.x (Latest) \- UCC Framework: 6.5.2 \- Python: 3.12 / 3.13 \- AppInspect: 0 errors, 0 warnings


Description:
App Purpose TA-suhlabs-eMASS is a Splunk Technology Add-on that ingests Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M) data from the Enterprise Mission Assurance Support Service (eMASS) API into Splunk. Problem/Situation Addressed Organizations using eMASS for cybersecurity compliance and risk management face several challenges: Data Silos: Security compliance data resides in eMASS while operational security data lives in Splunk, creating fragmented visibility across the security program. Manual Reporting: Security teams must manually extract POA&M data from eMASS to create reports, analyze trends, or correlate vulnerabilities with other security events - a time-consuming and error-prone process. Limited Analytics: eMASS provides compliance tracking, but lacks the advanced analytics, correlation, and visualization capabilities needed for comprehensive security operations and risk analysis. Compliance Monitoring: Organizations need real-time monitoring of their security posture and remediation progress, but accessing this data requires switching between multiple systems.

Release Notes:
## SCIP v1.2.10 — FedRAMP VDR/VER Reporting and PCI DSS 4.0.1 Compliance Accuracy Remediation Cumulative release covering all changes since v1.2.5 (build 247). Adds FedRAMP Vulnerability Detection and Response (VDR) / Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting (VER) support to the Monthly ConMon Package Builder, and remediates eleven compliance-accuracy defects identified by audits against the published PCI DSS v4.0.1 standard and FedRAMP's current continuous-monitoring rules. **SCIP-141 — FedRAMP VDR/VER reporting:** * New FedRAMP VDR/VER Vulnerability Report section in the Monthly ConMon Package Builder, reframing KEV-matched vulnerabilities from the BOD 26-04 classification engine into FedRAMP's VER language: exploitability (LEV/NLEV), internet reachability (IRV/NIRV), Potential Agency Impact N-rating (PAIN, N1-N5), and the mitigation/remediation timeframe (VDR-TFR-PVR). Implements the eleven required reporting items of VER-RPT-VDT and is exportable for monthly human-readable reporting (VER-TFR-MHR). * New lookups/fedramp\_vdr\_ver\_pain\_matrix.csv (16 rows) with a selectable FedRAMP certification class, open and auditable against FedRAMP's own published timeframe tables. Certification class materially changes remediation windows (for a PAIN-4 internet-reachable finding: 8 days at Class B, 2 days at Class D). * Applications with no public-exposure tag are treated as internet-reachable rather than silently assumed safe — the conservative posture FedRAMP's model requires. Panels include an explicit proxy disclosure stating which values are provisional proxies (IRV from the customer-declared exposure tag, PAIN from BOD 26-04 technical impact) and which require provider attestation, so the report cannot be mistaken for an assessment SCIP is not in a position to make. * Reportable-incident candidates (VER-TFR-IRI) and findings approaching the 192-day accepted-risk threshold (VER-TFR-MAV) are surfaced directly. Mandatory for FedRAMP-certified offerings by December 7, 2026, with the grace period ending March 7, 2027, per FedRAMP Public Notice NTC-0014. **SCIP-139 — PCI DSS 6.3.3 gap assessment corrected to be severity-aware:** * The 6.3.3 compliance-gap assessment previously reported a Gap on any confirmed open CVE regardless of severity, overstating non-compliance against a standard that does not require it. Gap now triggers only on critical severity or a CISA Known Exploited Vulnerability of any severity; other confirmed open vulnerabilities report as Needs Review rather than a compliance gap. * Version-unconfirmed matches no longer produce a Gap on their own — they report as Needs Review (unconfirmed version matches), so a finding SCIP cannot confirm applies to the deployed version is not presented to an assessor as a failure. **SCIP-143 through SCIP-149 — PCI DSS v4.0.1 control-mapping accuracy:** * 12.3.3 and 12.3.4 corrected. Both shipped rows previously described variants of 12.3.4's subject, leaving 12.3.3's real requirement (cryptographic cipher suites and protocols reviewed at least every 12 months) unrepresented while a result was still reported against its identifier. The technology-review check is now correctly identified as 12.3.4, and 12.3.3 is present and honestly marked not assessed rather than reported against the wrong control. * 10.2.1 corrected to 10.2.1.1 to match the content actually assessed (individual user access to cardholder data) rather than the broader parent requirement. * 11.3.2 now discloses that Approved Scanning Vendor status is not verified by the check, so a Pass cannot be read as confirmation that an ASV performed the scan. * 6.4.1 now discloses that its manual-review path was effectively sunset on March 31, 2025 and that an automated solution is required per 6.4.2. * 10.7.1 now discloses that the requirement applies to service providers only, with 10.7.2/10.7.3 identified as the equivalents for all other entities. * Requirement-family titles corrected to the official PCI DSS v4.0.1 wording for Requirement 6 ("Develop and Maintain Secure Systems and Software") and Requirement 12 ("Support Information Security with Organizational Policies and Programs"). * Upgrade path: environments that ran an earlier build carry a stale compliance-status record for the previously mismapped 12.3.3 identifier. A scheduled cleanup removes exactly that one record on upgrade, then no-ops indefinitely. No customer action is required and nothing else in the collection is touched. **SCIP-140 — PCI DSS version labeling:** * Compliance framework labeling updated from "PCI DSS 4.0" to "PCI DSS 4.0.1" across all customer-facing and compliance-evidence surfaces, matching the current published standard. Internal framework identifiers are unchanged, so existing saved searches, lookups, and exports continue to work without modification. **SCIP-138 and SCIP-142 — bundled documentation:** * README detection-rule counts corrected to match the shipped rule set (10 AI/agentic threat detection rules, 9 MITRE ATLAS-mapped, in the summary; 66 rules, 57 ATLAS-mapped, in the detail section). * Stated minimum supported platform raised to Splunk Enterprise 9.4+ and Splunk Cloud. Splunk 9.2 and 9.3 have reached end of life; no functional change for environments already on a supported release. No licensing or crypto surface was modified. bin/scip\_license\_core.py and bin/scip\_ed25519\_verify.py are byte-identical to baseline.

item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) — Release notes What's new, improved, and fixed in each release, in plain language. This is the **customer-facing** summary used for the Splunkbase release-notes section; the full technical changelog lives in the project's detailed release notes. **Last updated:** 2026-08-07 > **About version numbers.** Releases once numbered 0.10–0.13 were renumbered to > 1.0–1.3 to reflect production maturity — no behaviour changed. The current release is > **2.2.2** — a maintenance release on top of **2.2.1**, itself a maintenance release on > **2.2.0**'s **Explain a SPL search**, and **2.1.0**'s **Fraud capability** and the **2.0 line** (the deterministic **ITSI Root > Cause Analysis** engine, **resource-consumption monitoring**, and **2.0.7**'s durable memory, > Scheduled Ask and governed integrations), which in turn built on > **1.8.5** (the **CIM Coverage Audit**), **1.8.4** (async playbook execution over MCP > plus the **Outcome Ledger** executive/audit dashboard), **1.8.3** > (a security‑hardening release: OWASP + dependency + anti‑ransomware audit), **1.8.2** (Splunk > Edge Processor data‑quality awareness and keyless Azure OpenAI authentication), **1.8.1** > (support‑diagnosis fixes) and **1.8.0** (agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs, > all‑tiers data‑quality checks, Splunk 10.x readiness, Dashboard Studio version‑awareness). The > **1.7.0** ServiceNow integration and the **1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth"** themes are > included below. --- ## 2.2.2 "Finish the dashboard" A maintenance release about one thing: runs that did all the work and then ended with nothing on the glass. Every item came from watching real dashboard builds on a live estate, and in each case the assistant's own safety check was the reason the dashboard never appeared. The check was right about the problem and wrong about what to do next — it refused, gave instructions, and the instructions either could not be carried out or cost more of the run's budget than was left. ### Fixed - **Dashboards that were refused are now repaired instead.** When two panels ran the same underlying search, the assistant used to stop and describe a three-step manual fix. The fix is mechanical, so the builder now performs it: it creates the shared search once, points both panels at it, and keeps the fields those panels need. Your dashboards get the efficient shape without the run being interrupted, and the same search no longer runs twice. - **Panels that came back empty next to a search that clearly had data.** When a shared search was widened more than once to serve different panels, each widening discarded the previous one. On one nine-panel dashboard five panels showed "No results found" while the search behind them returned the right events. The widenings now combine. - **A check that asked for the impossible.** A panel that calculates its own value — a formatted date, a derived score — was refused for not finding that value in the shared search, where it cannot exist, because the panel computes it afterwards. Values a panel makes for itself are no longer demanded of the search. The related guidance was also wrong in a way that mattered: panels sharing a search are siblings, not a sequence, so a value one panel calculates is invisible to the others and has to be calculated where all of them can see it. - **A failed publish threw away the work it told you to fix.** The message on a validation failure said the dashboard was still open for editing and warned against starting over. It had in fact been discarded, so the repair failed and the assistant rebuilt every panel from scratch — which on one run quietly changed a correct detection into a different one. The dashboard now genuinely stays open when publishing fails. - **One special character could cost an entire dashboard.** A "≥" written as `≥` in a panel's explanatory text made the whole dashboard invalid, discarding a run of around forty steps that had already produced four working searches. Special characters in text are now handled safely no matter which one is used. - **An empty shared-search reference was treated as a real one**, producing a confusing refusal at publish time that asked for a search with a blank name. ### Improved - **Detections are now held to what you asked for.** New guidance covers the ways a detection can look perfect and point at the wrong event — quietly matching a wider set of events than you described, being loosened until it finally returns a row, discarding the field that distinguishes one event type from another, or dropping the amounts and account numbers an analyst needs before the result reaches the table. A rule that renders beautifully and flags the wrong event is worse than one that returns nothing, because nothing looks broken and nobody checks. The assistant now reads its own result back against the raw events before handing it to you. - **"No results" is no longer accepted as proof a detection works.** For a rule whose job is to match something, an empty result proves only that the syntax is valid — "this does not happen in your data" and "this rule cannot detect it" look identical. The assistant now establishes which of the two it is found before telling you, and runs over a period that actually covers the evidence it has already located. - **Sequence detections ("A, then B, then C") are built correctly.** A common shortcut for expressing order silently sorts alphabetically instead of by time, which can make a rule return nothing on a textbook-perfect match. Ordering is now derived from timestamps. ### Changed - **"Create / Update user template" are now "Create / Update user playbook"**, matching the Playbooks tab they belong to. Existing private playbooks you authored are unaffected; the old entries are retired so you are not offered both. --- ## 2.2.1 "Proven" A maintenance release, and every item in it came from running 2.2.0 against a real estate rather than from reading the code. One new capability came along with the fixes. ### Fraud rings your risk threshold cannot see (Enterprise, fraud-analytics) Risk-based alerting adds up one entity's score across many events. A fraud ring is the opposite shape: many entities sharing one thing. Because those are different questions, no amount of threshold tuning finds a ring. Seventeen mule accounts each earning fifteen points against a threshold of forty are seventeen well-behaved customers, since the risk was split seventeen ways and no single account ever crossed. Lower the threshold and you get seventeen false positives, not one ring. This release adds the query that asks the other question: group by the shared attribute instead of by the account. Nothing new has to be collected, because fraud risk rules have always recorded the linking attribute alongside the score. It simply was never read back this way. It is rarity-weighted, which matters more than it sounds. Ask only "what is shared" and the answer is always the corporate proxy that everybody sits behind. Imports live on the **Backups** page, which also shows which content version you're currently on — run a backup first and you can roll back in one click. - **Retire without deleting.** A pack can mark an item **retired** — it stays installed but is hidden and switched off everywhere (it can't be picked, run, or used by the assistant). An admin can re-enable it at any time by removing the tag. **Improved — data-quality checks for everyone, and Splunk 10.x readiness.** - **Data-quality ingestion checks are now available on every edition, including the free tier.** Checking whether a feed is actually landing and parsing correctly — on `index=_internal`, through **TrackMe**, and through **Cribl Stream** — is a baseline capability now, not a Professional add-on. - **Ready for Splunk Enterprise 10.2 and 10.4.** The app declares Python 3.9 **and** 3.13 compatibility and has been audited against the 10.x platform changes (dashboards, the web framework, KV Store). Your admin still completes the standard KV Store engine migration as part of any 10.x upgrade. - **Smarter Dashboard Studio building.** The assistant now works from a single, version-aware map of what Dashboard Studio supports on **your** Splunk version — it won't reach for a chart type your version can't render, and when your Splunk is newer than what we've documented it builds conservatively and verifies the result. **Fixed.** - **Fewer false "the dashboard is blank" errors.** A heavy Dashboard Studio dashboard that renders fine but slowly is no longer wrongly reported as blank — the assistant confirms the panels actually returned data before deciding, so it stops wasting a retry on a dashboard that was already correct. A genuinely blank dashboard is still caught. - **TrackMe panels only when they belong.** Fixed a rule that pushed a TrackMe feed-health panel onto every generated dashboard (and used a lookup that fails outside the TrackMe app). The assistant now adds a feed-health panel only when it's actually relevant, using a method that works in your app. --- ## 1.7.0 "ServiceNow integration" (included in the 1.8.0 release) > **Renamed to Adjutant AI.** The app is now **Adjutant AI** (formerly "AI Workbench"). > This is a **display-name change only** — the in-app title (the easter egg now lives on > the dot of the "i" in **Adjutant Ai**), the app label, the documentation, and the > assistant's own self-description all say **Adjutant AI**. Nothing functional changed: > the Splunk app id, your saved searches/dashboards/models, KVStore data, and generated > artifact names are unchanged, so the upgrade is seamless. **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other Splunk apps.** - **On a schedule or on an event.** A playbook can run **unattended** on a schedule (a "morning health check") or in response to a Splunk event — an alert, an ES correlation search, or an ITSI episode. When an event triggers it, the affected thing (the host, user, or entity in the alert) is handed to the playbook automatically, so it investigates exactly what fired. Two ready-made (disabled) examples are included to copy. - **Adjutant AI as a building block for other apps.** Other Splunk AI agents can now ask Adjutant AI to **list** and **run** your playbooks through a small, safe interface (an MCP server). Only playbooks you mark **MCPready** are exposed, every call must name the Org/BU it is for (which must be a business unit you have set up) as a safeguard, and runs go through the same governed, bounded service — never an open door. This interface is **off by default** — turn it on with one setting. When on, the tools can also appear inside **Splunk's own MCP Server**, reachable on the normal Splunk web address (no special port needed); you authenticate with a standard Splunk token. A ready-made, read-only **example playbook** ships enabled so there is always something to see the moment you switch the interface on. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** - One click on any conversation (per-turn 🐞, the Ask panel, or the new **Help tab**) packages exactly what happened — versions, the resolved prompt, the tools and model used, the generated dashboards/searches, and every error and warning — into a single file. - **Safe by construction:** secrets are stripped before anything leaves the browser, and the file is **encrypted** to the support key, so it's safe to send over any channel. - It even **tells you what kind of problem it looks like** and matches known issues, so simple cases are solved without a back-and-forth. - **Send it your way:** download it and attach it to your own ticket, use the built-in support form, or email it. The **Help tab** (Report + Documentation + About) is always reachable — even if the app is locked by licensing. **New — ServiceNow, done properly** (Professional + the `servicenow` feature). Read incidents, changes, problems and the **CMDB/CSDM** in plain English — with bounded blast-radius / dependency traversals ("what's the blast radius if this CI fails?"). Turn a Splunk alert, ITSI episode or ES notable into a rich, deterministically rendered ServiceNow incident and **write the number back** to the originating object (a re-fire updates, never duplicates; the closed-incident policy is configurable). **Security incidents (SIR)** with MITRE ATT&CK, off until an admin enables them. Two transports (REST **or** a ServiceNow MCP server), plus TISC threat-intel enrichment — all server-side and allowlisted, so ServiceNow can never block the assistant. *(Verified against the documented APIs and unit-tested; final certification is on a live ServiceNow.)* **New — run playbooks automatically, and from other apps.** Playbooks can run **unattended** on a schedule, or from a Splunk alert / ES correlation search / ITSI episode (the triggering entity is handed to the run). Adjutant AI can also expose **list / run** over an inbound **MCP server** (off by default, MCPready-only, Org/BU-scoped) — reachable inside Splunk's own MCP Server on the normal web address, with a standard Splunk token. **New — "Report an issue" support packaging (all editions).** One click packages a failing conversation — secret-stripped and **encrypted client-side** — with an automatic problem classification, plus an always-reachable **Help tab** even when the app is licence-locked. **New — Cribl Stream data-quality awareness** (Professional+). Reads Cribl's own forwarded logs and metrics to surface the timestamp / parse / dropped-event problems that happen *inside Cribl, before Splunk can see them* — the "green in Splunk but timestamped wrong" blind spot — folded into one readiness verdict. No Cribl Lake or Search required. **New — LLM reliability: retry, fallback & circuit breaker** (Enterprise). A brief provider hiccup (503 / 529 / rate-limit) auto-retries within a time budget; a per-config **circuit breaker** stops hammering a provider that's down, then probes for recovery; and an ordered **fallback** transparently switches to your next provider (and tells you which it used). Two new admin dashboards — **LLM Health** and **AI Activity** — plus per-user / BU / org concurrency caps, all conservative and off the critical path. **New — live model & cost catalogue (all editions).** Models and prices come from a runtime catalogue that updates without an app rebuild; **automatic model discovery** (Professional+) keeps it current without ever logging your keys; an Enterprise admin screen adds price overrides and manual model registration for private gateways. **Fixed.** Generated Simple XML dashboards now share a single base search across panels (faster) and get a top data-ingestion health panel; corrected a 3× Opus price over-charge (now server-side authoritative, with Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 included). --- ## 1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth" **New:** connect to **OAuth 2.1‑protected MCP servers** (authorization‑code + PKCE for interactive, client‑credentials for unattended; tokens held server‑side, never in the browser — see [MCP_OAUTH.md](MCP_OAUTH.md)); **onboard new data sources** — describe a source or attach a sample file and get a deployment‑ready add‑on package; a **"is my data parsed correctly?"** ingestion/timestamp check that reads Splunk's own internal logs; generated config **validated against your instance** and given a **0–100 Data Quality Score** (A–F); and attach a local sample file in Ask (only the file name is audited, never contents). **Improved:** works with the newest OpenAI "reasoning" models incl. Azure GPT‑5.4 / GPT‑5.4‑mini (auto‑detects the request format); more reliable generated dashboards; generated objects use the **`aiworkbench`** name tag; and Audit‑tab improvements (Business Unit column/filter, local‑timezone timestamps, reliable token/outcome capture). --- ## Earlier releases (1.0.0 – 1.4.3) - **1.4.3** — Clearer guidance and plain-language fixes when a free-tier LLM key hits its provider limits (e.g. Groq token-per-minute caps, Gemini zero-quota keys); the LLM config screen flags these up front. - **1.4.1** — Per-feature capability licensing with edition badges (Professional / Enterprise / MSP); gated features show a padlock, and nothing you created is ever deleted when a tier changes. Turn-level audit logging made reliable; more robust dashboard generation. - **1.4.0** — The assistant reads your own Splunk **live** (real search commands + installed visualizations) instead of guessing; Splunk Security Essentials detection content integrated. - **1.3.3** — TrackMe integration end-to-end (feed-health awareness + actions) with richer built-in platform knowledge. - **1.3.2** — First Splunkbase 1.x release: packaging and permissions hardening. - **1.3.1** — Fixed Org/BU edits dropping fields; safeguard to keep bundled playbooks correct after upgrades. - **1.3.0** — Real, per-Organisation audit logging of every AI interaction (Professional+). - **1.2.0** — Splunk Security Essentials content tools for playbooks. - **1.1.1** — Cisco Deep Time Series Model (CDTSM) playbooks: pre-trained anomaly detection and forecasting via the AI Toolkit, each with a proof dashboard. - **1.1.0** — Multi-tenancy and the Organisation / Business-Unit editor overhauled for clearer, safer tenant scoping. - **1.0.0** — The knowledge layer: ground answers in your organisation's own conventions. *(Releases before 1.0 are early pre-release history and are omitted here.)* --- ## Known issues - **Open the assistant from inside another app.** Adjutant AI is a "host shell": reach it from a navigation-menu entry inside Search, Enterprise Security, ITSI, or your own apps — not by clicking the app tile directly. Everything it creates lands in the namespace of the app you opened it from. - **Some Data Foundation features need self-hosted Splunk.** The configuration-reference grounding and config-package generation (1.5.0) read files on the Splunk server, so they are unavailable on Splunk Cloud; the assistant says so and continues with what it can. --- *When a published fix resolves a tracked GitHub issue, it is summarised here with its issue number — for example: "Fixed: a dashboard panel could display raw HTML markup as text instead of formatting it (#123)."*


Short Description:
A workbench for Splunk, not just a chatbot. Analyse, correlate and build across SPL, dashboards, alerts, AI Toolkit / MLTK, ES, ITSI and TrackMe through tools that understand each one — plus any MCP server you add. Pick your LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama, OpenRouter. Multi-tenant, multi-tier (Free, Pro, Enterprise, MSP).


Description:
Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) is a generative workspace for Splunk — not a chatbot bolted onto search, but a real workbench where you investigate, analyse and build with tools that understand Splunk. It is a host shell: it has no use-cases of its own, deriving everything from the Splunk app a user opens it from and their roles. Install once on the Search Head, then embed it in the apps your users already live in — Search, ITSI, Enterprise Security, your SOC and MSP customer apps. Users never leave the app they came from, and artefacts land in that app's namespace. Ask in plain English. Get back validated SPL, Simple XML and Dashboard Studio dashboards, alerts, lookups, reports and Splunk AI Toolkit (MLTK) machine-learning pipelines — grounded in your running Splunk (your knowledge objects, live command syntax, CIM models), run for real before they are saved, owned by the calling user. The depth is the difference. Where a generic MCP-only assistant talks to Splunk through one broad door, Adjutant AI ships fine-grained, Splunk-aware tools across Core, Enterprise Security, ITSI, TrackMe, ServiceNow and the AI Toolkit, each scoped to one job and run under your existing Splunk ACLs. Extend it with HTTP tools or any MCP server. New in 2.1 — a fraud capability that starts by telling you what you cannot yet detect. The Fraud Data Coverage Audit grades your estate against nine use cases (including AML) and returns ready, partial or blocked with the specific blocker, identifying event families by what events contain rather than by sourcetype name. Entity resolution runs before scoring, because risk accumulates per entity. Generated rules are weighted contributions with readable reasons, emitted into Enterprise Security's risk framework where it exists and into RBA's own field vocabulary where it does not. Nothing generated is ever enabled or scheduled. New in 2.0 — ITSI Root Cause Analysis with no LLM in the answer. It walks your real dependency graph, verifies the data behind every KPI, scores the evidence transparently, then lets an LLM narrate. The same evidence always gives the same answer. A red KPI on a dead feed is a data problem, and it names the forwarder, HEC, DB Connect, Cribl or Edge Processor leg at fault. Plus durable memory, scheduled playbooks, governed integrations, and per-tenant resource-consumption reporting. Your SOC can watch the agent: LLM calls, tool and ServiceNow calls, config changes, unattended verdicts and policy refusals emitted as OCSF events to an index Enterprise Security already watches. On-prem, no cloud egress, off by default. Bring your own LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama (fully offline) or OpenRouter — server-side, so keys never leave the search head. Multi-tenant by design. Free, Professional, Enterprise and MSP tiers, self-serve and air-gap-friendly.

Release Notes:
* Adds | honeylabssearch, a generating command that queries the honeypot dataset directly. * Nine modes: raw sensor events with every recorded field, literal substring search over captured request payloads, CVE exploitation, ASN profiles, attacker rankings, attack volume over time, and TLS, JA4, JA4H and SSH fingerprint searches. * Adds a second dashboard, Explorer, covering the dataset on its own terms.


Short Description:
Threat intelligence from live honeypot sensors, in SPL. Enrich any IP field with a verdict, ASN, ports and first and last seen, or query the dataset directly: raw probes, request payloads, CVE exploitation, JA4 fingerprints, top attackers. Plus two hourly threat feeds. Free API key gives 500 lookups a day; no key gives 10.


Description:
HoneyLabs runs open-source honeypot sensors on the public internet. Nothing reaches them by accident, so every connection they record is a scan, a probe, a brute-force attempt or an exploit. There are no false positives to filter out, because there is no legitimate traffic to confuse them with. This app puts that dataset inside Splunk. Two search commands. The first enriches addresses you already have. Point it at any field holding a public IPv4 address and it annotates every event: index=firewall | honeylabs field=src_ip | where honeylabs_events > 0 It writes back verdict, verdict_key, network_type, events, first_seen, last_seen, country, asn, asn_org, rdns, top_port, ports, exploit_hits and reference, each prefixed honeylabs_ so nothing collides with your own fields. Addresses are de-duplicated per search, so an index carrying the same scanner across ten thousand events costs one lookup. The second queries the honeypot dataset directly, with no local data required. Nine modes cover raw events, captured request payloads, top attackers, timelines, ASN profiles, TLS and HTTP fingerprints, IOC and CIDR lookups, CVE exploitation, and fingerprint population counts. Use it to answer questions your own logs cannot: who else is exercising this CVE, what payload is being sent, which other sources share this JA4 fingerprint. Two modular inputs, shipped disabled, index active exploiter addresses and captured malware staging URLs on an hourly schedule. Neither needs credentials. Two dashboards ship with the app: an overview of what the feeds currently carry, and an explorer for querying the dataset without writing SPL by hand. About the API key. The app installs and runs with no account and no setup, but anonymous use is capped at 10 lookups a day, which is enough to try the commands and not enough to work with. A free key raises that to 500 a day and takes about a minute to create at https://honeylabs.net/dashboard. Paste it into the app's setup page; it is stored through Splunk's storage/passwords, encrypted at rest, and never written to a .conf file. Paid plans go to 50,000 a day. On privacy: a lookup sends only the public IP addresses in your search. Not your index, host, source or sourcetype names, not your Splunk version, not the search string. Private, loopback, link-local, multicast and reserved addresses are filtered out locally before the request is built. The feed inputs are ordinary HTTPS downloads of a public file and disclose nothing at all. Running Enterprise Security? Load the indicator feeds through its own threat intelligence framework so they reach correlation searches and risk scoring rather than only being searchable, and keep these commands for on-demand investigation. Walkthrough: https://honeylabs.net/integrations/splunk-es

**### Version 2.1.4** \* **\*\*Fix: KV Store outage log clarity.\*\*** When Splunk KV Store is unavailable, checkpoint read/write now logs a clear warning instead of the misleading \`HTTPError\`/\`int\` TypeError from Splunk's helper. Collection continues using the configured start\_datetime window; restore KV Store for incremental checkpointing. **### Version 2.1.3** \* **\*\*Fix: Proxy lookup crash on Splunk 9 / Python 3.7.\*\*** \`get\_proxy()\` used \`rest.simpleRequest(..., raiseAllErrors\=True)\` without a top-level handler. When Splunk's REST layer failed, it could raise \`TypeError: '>\=' not supported between instances of 'HTTPError' and 'int'\`, aborting alert collection before any JupiterOne API call. Proxy lookup now uses \`raiseAllErrors\=False\`, validates status codes explicitly, and falls back to direct (no-proxy) requests. **### Version 2.1.2** \* **\*\*Fix: Deferred host resolution.\*\*** Host lookup no longer runs during input initialization (which triggered a GraphQL call before collection and could crash the entire run). Host is resolved at collection time from checkpoint, alert webLink, or base URL fallback. \* **\*\*Fix: Host fallback from GraphQL base URL.\*\*** When no checkpoint or sample alert exists, derive \`apps.\*\` host from the configured \`graphql.\*\` base URL so collection can proceed on fresh inputs. \* **\*\*Fix: Safer traceback formatting.\*\*** Guard against malformed tracebacks that caused \`TypeError: '>\=' not supported between instances of 'HTTPError' and 'int'\`. \* **\*\*Ops: Version marker in logs.\*\*** Each input run logs \`(TA version 2.1.2)\` so deployed builds are easy to verify. **### Version 2.1.1** \* **\*\*Fix: Alert collection HTTP error handling.\*\*** Replaced Splunk \`send\_http\_request\` (which raised \`HTTPError\` before status codes could be handled, and could mask the real error with a secondary \`TypeError\` during traceback formatting) with direct \`requests\` calls using the same proxy pattern as the JupiterOne search custom command. \* **\*\*Fix: Safe error trace logging.\*\*** Added defensive traceback formatting so HTTP and connection failures log the actual status code and response body instead of failing with \`'>\=' not supported between instances of 'HTTPError' and 'int'\`.

MITRE ATLAS is the adversarial threat matrix for AI/ML systems — the AI equivalent of MITRE ATT&CK. As organizations deploy LLMs, RAG pipelines, and ML APIs into production, they create an attack surface that most Splunk deployments have zero detection coverage for. This app provides 10 detection rules for AI and LLM threats — 9 mapped to specific MITRE ATLAS technique IDs, plus 1 vendor-defined rule where no canonical ATLAS technique covers the detection concept. When a data source goes silent — whether from a misconfigured forwarder, a failed log shipper, or a broken integration — Data Heartbeat detects the gap and alerts you before the silence becomes a blind spot. Every monitored source type has a configurable threshold, measured in minutes. When no data arrives within that window, the app flags the source type and fires your chosen alert action: Slack, Microsoft Teams, a generic webhook, or email via Splunk's built-in SMTP relay. Key features: • Monitor dashboard — a live status table showing every tracked source type, the minutes since its last event, its threshold, and its importance level, with color-coded severity (green, yellow, red, and critical). • Per-row alert actions — each source type can use its own notification target, independent of the global default. • Auto Discovery — a nightly scan that surfaces new source types appearing in your environment and queues them for review. • Importance tagging — mark business-critical sources as High, Medium, or Low importance. When a high-importance source goes silent, the app raises a red-alert banner. • Settings page — configure global defaults (threshold, alert action, and notification target), enable or disable the monitoring pipeline, and test alert actions without waiting for a real outage. • Audit log — a full history of every configuration change, with timestamps and user attribution. • No index footprint — all configuration is stored in KV Store, so no custom indexes are required.
